passage: In the colony sandpit, Ojas digs his own road right beside Rehana's castle, never touching it. He doesn't look at her, but he stays. "The blue bus goes from the market to the beach," he says, "and it has two doors, and the back door squeaks." Then he names every stop, in order, twice. Rehana pats sand onto her tower and listens. When her castle is done, Ojas quietly drives his toy bus right up to its gate and parks it there. "Bus stop," he says. Rehana grins. "Okay. My castle has a bus stop now."

qa.q: Where does Ojas park his toy bus?
qa.a: Right up to the gate of Rehana's castle.

qa.q: How does Ojas seem to feel about Rehana when he parks the bus at her castle?
qa.a: He seems friendly and eager to share his favourite thing with her, parking the bus at her gate even though he never looks at her.

qa.q: Which choice by Rehana kept the play going?
qa.a: She kept listening to the bus stops instead of walking off, and she welcomed the bus stop into her castle.

qa.q: How might Rehana see Ojas's play after the bus stop moment?
qa.a: She may realise he was playing with her all along, just side by side instead of face to face.

grounding: It shows a child who plays beside another child and talks at length about a favourite subject, and whose way of connecting is real.

passage: "Ammi, first teeth, then milk, then blue socks." "Shalini, today milk first. The van comes early." "No. Teeth first. Teeth, milk, socks." Her hands flap near her ears. Rehana kneels. "Okay, beta. Show me the chart." Shalini runs to the fridge and taps the picture cards. "Teeth. Milk. Socks. Shoes. Van." "Teeth it is. Super-fast teeth?" "Super-fast teeth." She brushes, gulps the milk, pulls on the socks. At the gate she tugs Rehana's sleeve. "Ammi, tomorrow is Saturday. Saturday chart is different. Saturday has park." "I know. You remind me." "I always remind you." She presses her cheek against Rehana's arm, once, then climbs into the van.

qa.q: What is the order on Shalini's morning chart?
qa.a: Teeth, milk, socks, shoes, van.

qa.q: Why does Shalini flap her hands when Rehana says milk first?
qa.a: The change to her set order upsets her; she needs the morning to go in the order she knows.

qa.q: What turning point in the morning made things go smoothly?
qa.a: Rehana asked to see the chart and followed it, making it a game with super-fast teeth instead of arguing.

qa.q: What would change if Rehana had insisted on milk first?
qa.a: Shalini would likely have become more upset, and they might have missed the van and the cheek-press goodbye.

grounding: It shows a child who needs a set order for the day and connects with her mother in her own real way.

passage:
Monday: At the play corner Yogesh, five, built a long line of blocks right next to Harsha's tower. He never touched the tower, but he stayed beside it all morning.
Thursday: Yogesh told Harsha about moths for a long time: their feathery feelers, the ones that look like leaves, the ones that fly only at night. Harsha listened, then wandered off to the swings.
Next Tuesday: Harsha ran in waving a drawing. "I made you a leaf moth!" Yogesh took it, sat next to Harsha and pointed at every part, grinning.

qa.q: What did Yogesh build on Monday?
qa.a: He built a long line of blocks right next to Harsha's tower.

qa.q: How can you tell Yogesh felt happy when Harsha brought the drawing?
qa.a: He took the drawing, sat next to Harsha and pointed at every part, grinning, which shows he was delighted and felt connected.

qa.q: What helped the two boys connect in the end?
qa.a: Harsha joined Yogesh's favourite subject by drawing a leaf moth, which gave them something real to share.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Yogesh after the moth talks?
qa.a: Harsha may see Yogesh as a friend who knows amazing things, even though Yogesh plays beside rather than with others.

grounding: Shows a child who plays beside others and talks at length about a favourite subject, whose way of connecting is real.

passage: The school picnic was cancelled at the last minute because of heavy rain, and Payal, six, stood in the hallway clutching her picture timetable: bus, park, lunch, home. "Picnic is today," she kept saying. Her older brother Kiran knelt with a pencil. "Let's make a new one. Rain, snack, drawing, home." Payal watched him cross out the bus, then pointed at the new boxes one by one and breathed out. At drawing time she did not join the other children's game but sat beside them, telling Kiran everything about volcanoes.

qa.q: Why was the school picnic cancelled?
qa.a: It was cancelled at the last minute because of heavy rain.

qa.q: How did Payal feel when the picnic was called off, and what calmed her?
qa.a: She felt upset and unsettled because her set order for the day was broken; she relaxed once Kiran made a new timetable with her.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that helped Payal?
qa.a: He gave her a clear new order for the day on paper instead of just telling her to be flexible.

qa.q: How might Kiran experience Payal's long talk about volcanoes?
qa.a: Kiran may feel close to Payal, knowing that sharing her favourite subject is her real way of connecting with him.

grounding: Shows a child who needs a set order for the day, plays beside others and talks at length about a favourite subject, with the rain adding a constraint.

passage: In the colony park in Chembur, the boys were playing cricket. Nilesh, five, walked the edge of the pitch reciting bus numbers: "Three-forty, three-forty-one, three-forty-two." Deepak's mother frowned. "Why won't he play properly?" Nilesh's Aaji smiled. "He's playing. Watch." Nilesh sat beside Deepak in the sand while Deepak dug a hole, and dug his own hole next to it. Later he held out a crumpled bus ticket from his pocket collection. Deepak took it carefully. "Can I have the blue one tomorrow?" Nilesh nodded hard.

qa.q: What was Nilesh reciting as he walked the edge of the pitch?
qa.a: He was reciting bus numbers: three-forty, three-forty-one, three-forty-two.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's hard nod suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he was happy and pleased that Deepak wanted another ticket from his collection, a sign he enjoyed their connection.

qa.q: How did Aaji help Deepak's mother see Nilesh differently?
qa.a: She calmly said he was playing and asked her to watch, instead of apologising for him or making him join the cricket.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Nilesh after getting the ticket?
qa.a: Deepak may see Nilesh as a friend with interesting treasures, and want to keep sitting and sharing with him.

grounding: Shows a child who plays beside others and talks about a favourite subject, whose different way of connecting is still real.

passage:
"Vishal, do you know volcanoes have magma chambers? And lava can be as hot as a very hot oven, and some volcanoes are under the sea, and—"
"Yusuf, do you want to play blocks?" Vishal asked.
Yusuf sat down next to Vishal and built his own tower, talking about volcanoes the whole time.
"Now snack," said Miss Rao.
"No! First blocks, then story, then snack!" Yusuf covered his ears.
"Okay, Yusuf. Blocks, story, snack." He lowered his hands.
Later Vishal said, "Miss, Yusuf didn't play with me."
Miss Rao smiled. "He sat next to you all morning and told you his favourite things. That's his way of being friends."

qa.q: What order did Yusuf want for the morning?
qa.a: First blocks, then story, then snack.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf cover his ears when Miss Rao said snack?
qa.a: He felt upset and anxious because the order he needed for his day was changing.

qa.q: How could an adult help Vishal understand Yusuf?
qa.a: Like Miss Rao, they can explain that sitting close and sharing favourite things is Yusuf's real way of connecting.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel after Miss Rao's explanation?
qa.a: Vishal might feel less left out and see that Yusuf was being friendly, just differently.

grounding: Yusuf plays beside Vishal, talks at length about volcanoes and needs a set order for the day, and his way of connecting is real.
